clinician.trajectory_summary: A 21-year-old woman presented with 3 weeks of subjective visual impairment and blurry vision. Prior examination by 2 other ophthalmology departments found no abnormalities, and she was initially misclassified as having psychosomatic disturbances. On current ophthalmologic examination, visual acuity was objectively normal (6/6 bilaterally on Snellen charts), with normal color vision (Ishihara), normal pupillary reflexes, normal anterior segment, normal fundus examination, normal visual fields (Humphrey full field 120), and normal fluorescein angiography and macular OCT. Brain MRI with contrast revealed 3 lesions not meeting diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis. Orbital MRI with contrast revealed no lesions. Spinal cord MRI revealed a lesion at the C3/C4 level extending over 3 vertebral segments, consistent with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM). The patient was treated with intravenous corticosteroids at 6 weeks after symptom onset. NMO-IgG serology was positive, confirming the diagnosis of Devic's syndrome (NMO spectrum disorder). At 4-year follow-up, visual function remained relatively preserved (6/9 bilaterally), but the patient developed urinary incontinence and walking disorders, reflecting progressive myelopathic complications.
